title: CSS Syntax & Rules 📜
description: Selectors, declarations, properties, values – break down a CSS rule piece by piece.

slides.title: Anatomy of a CSS Rule 🧬
slides.content:
# The Rule Set

A CSS rule consists of:
- **Selector** – targets HTML element(s).
- **Declaration block** – enclosed in curly braces `{ }`.
- **Declaration** – a property‑value pair followed by a semicolon.

```css
h1 {
  color: blue;
  font-size: 24px;
}
```
- `h1` is the selector.
- `color: blue;` is a declaration (property `color`, value `blue`).
- `font-size: 24px;` is another.

slides.title: Selectors: Targeting Elements 🔍
slides.content:
# Many Ways to Select

- **Type selector:** targets tag name, e.g., `p { }`.
- **Class selector:** targets elements with a specific class, e.g., `.highlight { }`.
- **ID selector:** targets a unique element, e.g., `#logo { }`.
- **Universal selector:** `* { }` selects everything.

Multiple selectors can share the same rule by separating with commas:
```css
h1, h2, h3 {
  font-family: sans-serif;
}
```

quizData.question: What character prefixes a class selector in CSS?
quizData.explanation: A dot (.) before a name indicates a class selector, e.g., `.btn`.

slides.title: Properties and Values 📏
slides.content:
# The Style Instructions

CSS has hundreds of properties, each accepting specific value types. Values can be keywords, lengths, colours, percentages, etc.

```css
p {
  margin: 10px 0;       /* shorthand for top/bottom 10px, left/right 0 */
  text-align: center;   /* keyword value */
  color: #333333;       /* hex colour */
}
```
Always end each declaration with a semicolon. While the last one is technically optional, omitting it can cause errors when adding more rules later.

slides.title: Putting It Together
slides.content: A CSS snippet with multiple rules:

quizData.question: In the rule `h2 { color: green; }`, the term 'color' is a ______.
quizData.explanation: `color` is the CSS property; `green` is its value.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Keep Selectors Simple

Avoid overly complex selectors at first. Rely on classes for styling and IDs for unique elements. This keeps your CSS maintainable.
